name: Eutropoflavin (7,8-DHF)

lead: 7,8-DHF is a flavone reported in 2010 to mimic BDNF signalling at the TrkB receptor. Nootropic enthusiasts take it for mood, cognition and recovery; the payoff is general wellbeing and drive rather than a direct change in how you look.

It is described as binding TrkB and triggering signalling such as AKT, though a 2017 line of work questioned direct agonism. All published work found is in cells and animals, with low oral bioavailability in mice, and no human trial was found.

paras: People take it as capsules, often as part of a nootropic stack, and judge it by mood, focus and how recovered they feel over a few weeks. The name eutropoflavin is used in forums for 7,8-DHF, though references apply it to a related analogue.
No human safety data were found. Some in vitro effects, such as weak aromatase inhibition, have not been confirmed in living animals. It is not an approved drug.

angle.text: 7,8-DHF is used by nootropic enthusiasts as a BDNF mimic for mood, cognition and recovery, with the appearance link being general wellbeing and drive. It has been studied in cells and animals; no human studies exist.

lead: 7,8-Dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), also called tropoflavin, is a naturally occurring flavone found in plants such as Godmania aesculifolia, Tridax procumbens and Primula vulgaris. It was reported in a 2010 PNAS paper as a small-molecule agonist of TrkB, the main receptor for brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) [1].

Sources differ on naming. Wikipedia uses the name eutropoflavin for the analogue 4'-dimethylamino-7,8-dihydroxyflavone [1], while Grokipedia applies it to that analogue as a synthetic compound reported from Emory University work [2]. Supplement and forum use often applies the name to 7,8-DHF itself. Research is limited to cells and animals; no human clinical study was found.

paras: 7,8-DHF was described as a selective TrkB agonist with a dissociation constant of roughly 320 nM, and also as having antioxidant activity said to be independent of TrkB [1]. A 2017 line of work suggested it and other reported small-molecule TrkB agonists might not act as direct TrkB agonists [1]. In mice it is orally bioavailable (about 5%) with an elimination half-life under 30 minutes and crosses the blood-brain barrier [1]. The prodrug R13 has improved pharmacokinetics and is under development for Alzheimer's disease [1].

Reported animal-model results span depression, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's, Huntington's, ALS, traumatic brain injury, stroke, fragile X and Rett syndrome, plus improved memory in healthy rodents [1]. In mice it reduced dark-phase sleep and hypothalamic orexin A [1]. Grokipedia reports that the 4'-dimethylamino analogue promoted hippocampal neurogenesis and reduced immobility in forced-swim tests in mice [2]. In vitro it is a weak aromatase inhibitor, an effect not confirmed in vivo [1].

timeline.event: 7,8-DHF reported as a small-molecule TrkB agonist [1]
